activities.name: Flying Numbers
activities.setup: Mark space with cones, small goals on both sides. Two teams along the touchline either side of you. Call a number combo (1v1, 2v1, 2v2, 3v2) and each side sends in that number to scrimmage. New players rotate in after every goal or ball out. Call different numbers from each side to create imbalanced situations.
activities.look_for: The most adaptable game in the toolkit. If one player is dominating, play them 1v2. If a quieter player needs more touches, play the ball directly to them. You control the challenge level in real time. Works perfectly as an anchor activity because it never feels the same twice.
activities.question: When you had more players than the other team, what did you do with that extra person?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 2 goals · Disc cones · Pinnies

u12.setup: Mark space with cones, goals on both sides. Two teams along the touchline either side of you. Call a number combo and each side sends in that number to scrimmage. New players rotate in after every goal or ball out. Frame the transition explicitly: outgoing players sprint off, incoming players sprint on. No walking at any point.
u12.look_for: The most adaptable game in the toolkit and the best anchor activity at U12. Works as pure anchor (high energy, familiar) or as a transition focus when you emphasize the urgency of sprinting in and out. If one player is dominating, play them 1v2.
u12.question: When you had more players than the other team, what did you do with that extra person?

activities.name: Shrinking Field
activities.setup: Rectangular grid with goals at each end. 3v3 or 4v4. Every minute, move each touchline in by 3 steps. The field narrows progressively. Players must make decisions faster as space disappears. Team with most goals after 3 minutes wins the round. Play 2–3 rounds.
activities.look_for: Players whose first touch opens their body, hips at 45 to 90 degrees toward goal, have more time in tight spaces. Players who receive square-on get pressed immediately. On the second visit, frame it as a defending focus: which team stays compact and presses together as the field shrinks?
activities.question: As the field got smaller, what changed about when you decided to pass?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 2 goals · Disc cones

activities.name: 1v1 to Endlines & Goals
activities.setup: 1v1 to Endlines: small rectangle, score by dribbling ball over opponent’s end line within arm’s distance. Progress to 1v1 to Small Goals: add cone goals at each end, score below knee height. Pairs run simultaneously. Fast rotations. Keep multiple pairs active at once.
activities.look_for: At U10 the focus shifts: not just beating the defender, but the decision: dribble or shoot? When is each the right answer? Players who look up to check for the goal before driving are already thinking ahead. Works well as an anchor because every player is active simultaneously.
activities.question: When you got past your opponent, what made you decide to shoot rather than keep dribbling?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per pair · 4 cones per game · Pinnies · Small goals optional

u8.setup: Pairs working in rectangles about 10 by 15 yards. 1v1 to Endlines: players score by dribbling the ball over their opponent's end line with the ball within arm's reach of their body. No shooting, so more touches and more decisions. Progress to 1v1 to Cone Goals: add a cone goal at each end and players score by kicking through below knee height. Run all pairs simultaneously. Fast rotations keep everyone active.
u8.look_for: Players trying to dribble past the defender rather than just kicking and chasing. Reward the attempt regardless of outcome. If players are unevenly matched, play the ball directly to the less skilled player to level the challenge.
u8.question: When you had the ball, did you try to go past your opponent or around them? What worked?

activities.name: Rondo
activities.setup: Square grid, one defender in the center, four attackers on the outside. This is called a rondo. Attackers keep the ball away from the defender. When the defender wins it or the ball goes out, the attacker who last touched it swaps into the middle. Keep track of consecutive passes. Progress: add a second defender (4v2) if passing is excellent, or drop to 3v1 to force attackers to move more.
activities.look_for: Look for attackers spreading out to give the player with the ball multiple options. Players who bunch together make the defender's job easy. The player with the ball should always have at least two teammates they can see. On the receiving end, open hips give a player more time before the defender closes in.
activities.question: When you were in the middle defending, what made it harder to win the ball? What made it easier?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per group · 4 cones per square · Pinnies for defenders

activities.name: Gates Passing
activities.setup: Rectangular grid with 8–10 gates scattered throughout (two cones arm’s length apart). Players in pairs with one ball. Score by passing to each other through gates. After passing, move immediately to a new gate. Encourage players to tell their partner where they are going before they pass.
activities.look_for: The pass-and-move habit is the entire point. A player who passes and stands still is not learning “Me & My Teammates.” Look for any player who moves after passing. Name it when you see it. Also look for open body shape on receiving. Progress: replace the gates with cone triangles scattered around the grid. Players score by passing through a triangle to their partner. Now add a challenge: tell your partner where you are going before you pass. The pair that communicates most will score the most.
activities.question: After you passed the ball, what did you do next? Why does moving matter?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per pair · 8–10 tall cone gates · Disc cones for grid

variants.name: Triangle Goal Game
variants.note: Progression: replace the gates with cone triangles. Players score by passing through a triangle to their partner.

activities.name: End Zone Passing
activities.setup: Rectangular grid with a small end zone marked at each end (about 4 yards deep). Two teams of 3 or 4. Players can dribble freely in the middle of the field, but the only way to score is to pass the ball to a teammate who has run into the opponent's end zone to receive it. The receiver must have both feet inside the end zone when they catch the ball.
activities.look_for: This game makes movement off the ball essential. A team that stands still cannot score because no one is in the end zone to receive. Look for players who time their run to arrive as the ball is being played. Any player who calls for the ball while running into the end zone is showing real game intelligence. Celebrate those moments explicitly.
activities.question: When did you run into the end zone? What were you watching to know when to go?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · Disc cones for grid and end zones · Pinnies

activities.name: Numbers Passing
activities.setup: Grid with 4 cones. Assign each player a number, their passing order. Players jog around the space passing in numbered order: 1 to 2, 2 to 3, until the last number passes back to 1. Add a second ball when they find a rhythm. Optional: add a goal. The last player shoots, then becomes the new number 1.
activities.look_for: Look for players keeping hips open (not square-on), cushioning the ball softly, then taking a purposeful next touch. Players who are always looking for the next number before the ball arrives will stand out. That anticipation is body shape doing its job. Works well as a focus activity after Gates Passing.
activities.question: How did you know where the next number was before the ball came to you?
activities.equipment: 1 ball (2 when ready) · Disc cones for grid

activities.name: 2v2 to Endlines — Attacking
activities.setup: Small rectangular space. Two attackers vs two defenders. Attackers score by dribbling ball over opponent’s end line within arm’s distance. Defenders can steal and score too. Rotate new players when scoring or ball out. Keep it fast. Run multiple games simultaneously.
activities.look_for: Encourage the attacker with the ball to drive at one defender to commit them, while the second attacker finds open space. When they spread out and use that advantage, celebrate it. The moment a player passes around a committed defender, even once, is worth highlighting for the whole group.
activities.question: When you had the ball and a defender coming at you, what options did you have?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per game · 4 cones per game · Pinnies

activities.name: 3v2 to Goal
activities.setup: Rectangular grid, small goal at one end. Three attackers from one end meet two defenders. Attackers work together to score. Defenders can score by dribbling over the end line. Remind attackers to spread out. Rotate defenders so they don’t get discouraged.
activities.look_for: Do not explain the combination in advance. Run the game and watch it emerge. If a player dribbles at a defender to force commitment and then passes around them, freeze the moment briefly: “Did everyone see that? What happened there?” That is the whole concept in one moment.
activities.question: When did you decide to pass rather than keep dribbling? What did you see that told you to pass?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 1 small goal · Disc cones · Pinnies

activities.name: Five Goal Game
activities.setup: Rectangular grid with a cone goal in each corner plus one in the center, 5 goals total. 3v3 or 4v4. Players try to pass the ball through any goal to a teammate to score in any direction. Defenders protect all 5 goals and can only gain possession by intercepting or stealing.
activities.look_for: Attackers must adapt quickly when their path is blocked. Players without the ball must move to open space near goals so their teammate has someone to find. Best as a focus activity later in the season when combination play is starting to click.
activities.question: When the goal you were aiming for was blocked, what did you do?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 5 goal pairs (4 corners + 1 center) · Pinnies

u12.setup: Rectangular grid with a cone goal in each corner plus one in the center, 5 goals total. 3v3 or 4v4. Players try to pass the ball through any goal to a teammate to score in any direction. Defenders protect all 5 goals and can only gain possession by intercepting or stealing.
u12.look_for: At U12 this game requires players to read the whole picture: all five goals, where teammates are, where defenders are. Watch for players who signal to a teammate where they are switching before the ball arrives. That anticipation is team play at its most sophisticated. Also watch for immediate transition reactions on every turnover.
u12.question: When you changed which goal you were going for, did your teammate know before you passed, or after?

activities.name: Barcelona
activities.setup: Rectangular grid with goals at each end. 3v3 or 4v4, no goalkeeper. Score points equal to the number of passes completed before scoring: 8 passes before a goal = 8 points. A missed shot scores nothing. Play short rounds of 3–4 minutes.
activities.look_for: Teams that learn to move the ball patiently before shooting will outscore teams that rush. Watch for players who switch the ball to the far side before going to goal. That is combination play at its most sophisticated. Best as a focus activity late in the season when passing habits are forming.
activities.question: Before you scored, was there a moment where you switched the ball to the other side? What did that open up?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 2 small goals · Disc cones · Pinnies

u12.setup: Rectangular grid with goals at each end. 3v3 or 4v4, no goalkeeper. Score points equal to the number of passes completed before scoring: 8 passes before a goal = 8 points. A missed shot scores nothing. Play short rounds of 3 to 4 minutes.
u12.look_for: Watch for players who switch the ball to the far side before going to goal, drawing defenders before finding the opening. Celebrate it when it happens by name. Best as a focus activity, not an anchor.
u12.question: Before you scored, was there a moment where you switched the ball to the other side? What did that open up?

activities.name: Rondo 5v2
activities.setup: Square of cones. Five attackers in a circle, two defenders in the center. Attackers keep the ball away. Track consecutive passes. Attacker who last touched an interception or ball out of bounds swaps with a defender. Rotate defenders every few minutes. Limit to 1–2 touches for extra challenge.
activities.look_for: Where the Rondo (4v1) is a small tight game, this is the bigger version: more players, two defenders, faster decisions required. Quick touches and spreading the space are the two things to reinforce. Encourage attackers to draw a defender toward them before passing. The moment a defender commits, there is a free player somewhere. That read is the whole game.
activities.question: How did you draw the defender in before passing? What would have happened if you passed straight away?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 4 cones for square · Pinnies for defenders

activities.name: Approach & Delay
activities.setup: Rectangular grid about 10 by 15 yards. An attacker with the ball starts at one end line, a defender starts 5 yards away. The attacker scores by dribbling over the far end line. The defender wins by taking the ball or knocking it out. Rotate after every turn. Teach one picture: run at the ball quickly, then slow down as you arrive, with the body turned a little to the side.
activities.look_for: Fast approach, slow arrival. A defender who lunges and gets dribbled past has learned something too. Name the player who slows down and stays on their feet, even if the attacker gets by. Delaying is a win at this age. Progress: add a second defender who starts behind the first and calls “cover.”
activities.question: When you got close to the dribbler, what did you do with your feet and your speed?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per group · Disc cones for the grid · Pinnies

activities.name: Pressure & Cover 3v3
activities.setup: Grid about 25 by 20 yards with three cone gates on one end line. Attackers (3) score by passing or dribbling through any gate. Defenders (3) win the ball and play it out across the opposite end line. Before each round, defenders name who is first (presses), who is second (covers), and who is third. Freeze the game once or twice per round and ask each defender where they are standing.
activities.look_for: The second defender stands behind and to the side of the first, close enough to step in if they are beaten. Look for the defender who steps in after a teammate is dribbled past instead of watching. Look for players who talk: “I have cover.” Do not fix everything at once. Pick one picture per round.
activities.question: When your teammate pressed, where did you stand? What did you do when they got beaten?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 3 gates (6 tall cones) · Disc cones for the grid · Pinnies

activities.name: Shadow Marking
activities.setup: Grid about 30 by 20 yards with a small goal at each end, no goalkeepers. 4v4. Give each defender one attacker to stay with (match pinnie colors or numbers). A goal counts double if the scoring player was marked closely, and an interception counts as a point. Everyone plays defender and attacker. Play two minutes per round, then swap who marks whom.
activities.look_for: Marking means staying between your player and the goal, close enough to step in when the ball is played. Look for defenders who keep one eye on the ball and one on their player. A defender who ball-watches loses their player. Celebrate the player who steps in front and steals the pass.
activities.question: When your player moved, how did you decide how close to stay?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 2 small goals · Disc cones · Pinnies in 2 colors, numbered if possible

activities.name: Squeeze the Space
activities.setup: Half field with a goal and a goalkeeper (or a large cone goal). Mark two wide channels, about 5 yards wide, along the sidelines. 5 attackers v 4 defenders. Attackers score from the middle or by crossing from a wide channel. Defenders start by getting narrow and close to the center, then shift toward the ball. Call “squeeze” and the defenders tighten up around the ball.
activities.look_for: Defenders closer together than they were a minute ago. A shape that shifts as the ball moves instead of chasing it. Watch for the wide defender who keeps the cross from being easy, and the players who block the shot instead of turning away. Winning the ball is a bonus. Making the shot hard is the goal.
activities.question: When the ball went wide, where did the rest of your team go?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 1 goal and keeper · Disc cones for channels · Pinnies

activities.name: Red Light Green Light
activities.setup: Grid about 25 by 20 yards. Every player has a ball. Green light: dribble fast. Yellow light: slow down with small touches to keep the ball close. Red light: stop with one foot on the ball. Call lights at random as players move around the grid. After a minute, ask players to suggest a new color and give it a new action (orange means swing your arms, purple means dance) and repeat each new color a few times.
activities.look_for: Players keeping the ball within arm's reach at yellow. Heads up to avoid collisions. On red light, emphasize using the sole of the foot to stop rather than letting the ball roll away.
activities.question: When I called yellow, what did you have to do with your feet to keep the ball close?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · Disc cones for grid

activities.name: 101 Dalmatians
activities.setup: Grid about 25 by 20 yards with small cone triangles scattered throughout, about one triangle per player. Every player has a ball. Players score by dribbling through a triangle with the ball within arm's reach of their body. Players count their own score out loud and shout it each time they hit a triangle. The group goal is 101 combined. Your job is to roam the grid and knock balls away, going after your stronger players first.
activities.look_for: Players using small touches to keep the ball close when you approach. Heads up to spot both the triangles and you coming. The counting keeps players invested in the team total.
activities.question: How did you keep the ball safe when I came near you?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · Disc cones for outer grid and inner triangles

activities.name: Wreck-It Ralph
activities.setup: Grid about 25 by 20 yards with a cone goal in each corner, opening inward. Every player has a ball. Players dribble around the grid and score by dribbling their ball through any corner goal while you (Wreck-It Ralph) roam and try to knock balls away. Ball knocked out: 10 toe taps to re-enter. Play short rounds of about a minute. Cone goals only, no small goals needed.
activities.look_for: Players who look up to find an open goal before driving toward it. That is scanning in action. Encourage players to beat their own score each round.
activities.question: Before you drove toward a goal, what did you check first?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · Disc cones for grid and corner goals

activities.name: Duck Tails
activities.setup: Grid about 20 by 20 yards. Every player has a ball and tucks a pinny in the back of their shorts. Players dribble around the space trying to steal a teammate's tail while protecting their own. Start with no elimination: if a tail falls off, tuck it back in and keep playing. For a final competitive round, switch to elimination: tail stolen means you are out. Last player with their tail wins. Count how many tails each player collects.
activities.look_for: Players who face their opponent rather than just running away. That is the beginning of how they will take on a defender. Heads up to see where tails are and where opponents are coming from.
activities.question: What did you do when someone came to steal your tail?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · Disc cones for grid · Pinnies as tails

activities.name: Knockout
activities.setup: Grid about 20 by 20 yards. Every player has a ball and dribbles freely. Players try to knock other players' balls out of the grid while keeping their own in. Ball knocked out: five toe taps outside the grid, then back in (non-elimination). For a final competitive round, switch to elimination: ball knocked out means you are out. Last player with their ball in the grid wins. Remind players to keep their ball close when an opponent approaches.
activities.look_for: Players who shield the ball with their body rather than just running away. Players who look up to track both the ball and the incoming threat.
activities.question: When someone came to knock your ball out, what did you do to protect it?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · Disc cones for grid

activities.name: Dinosaur Tag
activities.setup: No outer boundary needed. Each pair sets up a triangle of three cones, with sides about 5 yards long. One player is the dinosaur, one is the park ranger. Both dribble around their triangle. The dinosaur tries to tag the park ranger. The park ranger can go any direction around the triangle but cannot leave the ball. Switch roles after every tag or after one minute. Hissing by the dinosaur is strongly encouraged.
activities.look_for: Players learning to change direction quickly while keeping the ball close. Some players will struggle with the turns, and that is fine. Encourage small touches with both inside and outside of the foot. The competition drives the skill.
activities.question: What did you do with the ball when you needed to change direction quickly?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per pair · 3 cones per pair to form a triangle

activities.name: Gates Dribbling
activities.setup: Grid about 25 by 20 yards with 8 to 10 gates scattered throughout. Each gate is two tall cones placed an arm's length apart. Every player has a ball. Score a point by dribbling through any gate. 60-second challenge: how many gates can you get through? Tell players to imagine a force field the size of their arms, and the ball should stay inside it while they dribble. Progress: call a specific cone color and players must look up to find those gates first.
activities.look_for: Players who keep their head up find more gates. The game creates the need for scanning without you naming it. After the question, name it: "That looking up while you dribble is called scanning."
activities.question: How did you find the gates faster? What were you doing with your eyes?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · 8 to 10 tall cones in pairs · Disc cones for grid · Timer

activities.name: Shadow Dribbling
activities.setup: Grid about 25 by 20 yards. Players in pairs, each with their own ball. One player is the leader who dribbles however they want: fast, slow, turning, zigzagging. Their partner is the shadow, following close behind and mimicking every move. Switch roles every minute. If a leader tries something fancy, encourage the shadow to try it too even if it is not an exact copy.
activities.look_for: The shadow must have their head up to follow the leader. Players who look at their own ball fall behind. The game builds the reflex to look up naturally, without you ever asking for it.
activities.question: How did you stay close to your leader? What did you have to keep your eyes on?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · Disc cones for grid

activities.name: Color Tag Dribble
activities.setup: Grid about 25 by 20 yards with colored tall cones placed around the space. Every player has a ball and dribbles freely. Hold up a colored cone and all players must dribble to touch a cone of that color before you count to ten. Vary the colors and the pace. Progress: have two callers with different colors at the same time so players must split their attention.
activities.look_for: Players who keep their head up while dribbling reach the color fastest. Let the game teach the lesson. After the question, you can name it: "That is scanning."
activities.question: Who got to the cone fastest? What were you doing with your head while you were dribbling?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · Multiple colored tall cones · Disc cones for grid

activities.name: Shooting Gallery
activities.setup: Grid about 20 by 20 yards with a cone goal on the center of each side, all opening inward, four goals total. Every player has their own ball. Players dribble freely inside the grid and shoot at any goal they choose. After the shot, retrieve the ball and go again. No groups, no queues, everyone active the whole time. Challenge: how many different goals can you score on in 60 seconds?
activities.look_for: Players who look up to find an open goal before driving toward it. Volume of attempts is the point: confidence to shoot develops now and accuracy comes with time. Celebrate every goal. A player who scores on all four goals in one round deserves a big reaction.
activities.question: Before you shot, what did you look at?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per player · 8 tall cones for 4 goals (pairs, arm's length apart) · Disc cones for grid · Timer

activities.name: 2v1 to Goal
activities.setup: Groups of 3. Two attackers against one defender, attacking a cone goal about 6 yards wide. Ball starts with one attacker around 10 yards out. Rotate roles every 30 seconds. Run 2 to 3 groups simultaneously depending on how many adults are available to manage them. Do not coach the pass: let players discover the advantage of having a teammate free. Rotate defenders regularly so they do not get discouraged.
activities.look_for: Do not coach the combination. If a player passes to a free teammate and they score, celebrate it loudly and specifically: "Did everyone see that? Two players just solved a problem that one player couldn't." That moment is the first seed of Me & My Teammates.
activities.question: When you had two players against one defender, what options did you have? Did you use both of them?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per group · 2 tall cones per goal · Pinnies · Run 2 to 3 groups simultaneously

activities.name: Half and Half
activities.setup: Rectangular grid with goals at each end and a midpoint line of cones. 3v3 or 4v4. Normal scrimmage, except a goal only counts if the attacking team has at least one player in both their attacking AND defending halves when the goal is scored. The player who stays back is providing depth and defensive security.
activities.look_for: Forces players to spread across the length of the field, not just the width. The player who stays in the defending half might miss the goal celebration. Acknowledge them specifically. US Soccer introduces depth of shape explicitly at U12. This game teaches it without you naming it.
activities.question: The player who stayed back when your team scored: what were they protecting?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 2 small goals · Disc cones including midpoint line · Pinnies

activities.name: 3v3+1 Keep-Away
activities.setup: Square of cones for every 7 players. Two teams of 3 in different colors, one neutral player who plays with whoever has the ball. Attackers rack up passes. When defenders win it, the neutral player switches sides immediately. No delay. After a minute, switch roles.
activities.look_for: The neutral player switching sides instantly is the whole point. That instant role switch seeds transition awareness naturally inside a possession game. Also look for players opening their hips to receive before the ball arrives. Works well as Activity B after Flying Numbers.
activities.question: When the ball turned over, how quickly did you read whose team you were joining or defending against?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per grid · 4 cones per square · 3 colors of pinnies

activities.name: 2v2v2 Keep-Away
activities.setup: Square of cones for every 6 players. Three pairs in different colors. Two pairs attack and keep the ball away from the defending pair. When defenders steal or force a mistake, they replace the attacking pair who last touched the ball. Immediately, no stoppages. The new defenders must get into position fast.
activities.look_for: The defending pair must communicate constantly: who pressures the ball, who covers behind. Look for the pair who splits those jobs naturally. The team that defends compactly wins the ball most often.
activities.question: When you were the defending pair, how did you decide who would press the ball and who would cover?
activities.equipment: 1 ball per grid · 4 cones per square · 3 colors of pinnies

activities.name: Half Court Soccer
activities.setup: Rectangular grid, wider than it is long. A check line at one end, the goal at the other. Both teams attack the same goal, like half-court basketball. If a team steals the ball, they must clear it by dribbling over the check line before they can attempt to score. Play 3v3 plus an optional rotating goalkeeper.
activities.look_for: The check line creates a natural defending moment. Defenders must get compact between the ball and the goal. When the attack clears the line and comes back, defenders must re-organize quickly. Watch for players who position between opponent and goal rather than just chasing the ball.
activities.question: When the other team was dribbling toward goal, where were you standing? Between the ball and the goal, or somewhere else?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 1 goal · Disc cones including check line · Pinnies

activities.name: Shrinking Field: Defending Focus
activities.setup: Rectangular grid with small goals at each end. 3v3 or 4v4. Every minute, move each touchline in by 3 steps. Explicitly frame it as a defending focus before starting: "today we are watching the defending team, not the attacking team." Play 2 to 3 rounds.
activities.look_for: As the field shrinks, the compact defending shape becomes more and more important. Watch for the defending team getting tighter: closer together, higher up, forcing play to one side. Are they reacting to the ball or anticipating where it is going? Any moment of anticipation is worth highlighting.
activities.question: As the field got smaller, did defending get easier or harder? What does that tell you about defending in tight spaces?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 2 small goals · Disc cones

activities.name: Flying Numbers: Transition Focus
activities.setup: Same as the opening game anchor, but now explicitly framed around transition. Outgoing players must sprint off the field. Incoming players must sprint on. No walking at any point during rotation. Call the numbers quickly so there is barely any gap between rounds.
activities.look_for: The transition moment is the entire point. What happens the instant a goal is scored or the ball goes out? Do players react and sprint in, or shuffle in? Urgency in transition is a habit and habits form through repetition. This is why Flying Numbers appears in both the anchor and focus roles.
activities.question: What is the difference between a team that sprints into transition and a team that walks? How does that change what the other team can do?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 2 goals · Disc cones · Pinnies

activities.name: Crisscross
activities.setup: Square grid with a goal on the middle of each side, 4 goals total. One team scores on the two endline goals; the other scores on the two touchline goals. Play 2v2 or 3v3. Score by passing through a goal to a teammate. The cross-axis attack means defenders must constantly re-orient.
activities.look_for: Trains the transition instinct directly: the instant you win the ball, find the goal immediately. Players who hesitate give defenders time to recover. Players who look up the moment they win possession and find a goal in one or two actions are showing what the transition block looks like in practice.
activities.question: How quickly after winning the ball did you find your target? What would have happened if you waited two more seconds?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 4 cone goals (pairs, arm's length apart) · Pinnies

activities.name: Hawaii
activities.setup: Square grid. Two goals set back about 5 yards from each end, one per team. 3v3 or 4v4. Players can score on either goal on their end line but must shoot from inside the grid. Keep extra balls next to you and feed them in immediately after each score or out-of-bounds. Continuous play, no stoppages.
activities.look_for: The continuous play means players are constantly switching between attack and defense. Watch for who reacts instantly versus who celebrates and switches off. Relentless transitions make this the most game-realistic activity in this group.
activities.question: When a new ball came in while you were still celebrating a goal, how quickly did you switch back to defending?
activities.equipment: Multiple balls (keep several nearby) · 4 goals in 2 pairs · Disc cones · Pinnies

activities.name: Hotbox
activities.setup: Rectangular grid with a small goal at each end and a no-go square (the hotbox) in the center. 3v3 or 4v4. Players cannot enter the hotbox. Only balls can pass through. When the attackers' path is blocked by the hotbox and a defender on one side, the solution is to switch the ball to the other side.
activities.look_for: Naturally brings in all four blocks in a single activity: ball mastery under pressure, switching the point of attack, cutting off lanes around the hotbox, and instant reaction on turnover. Best used in week 7 to observe all four without isolating any one.
activities.question: When your path was blocked, what did you do? And when the ball turned over, what was your first movement?
activities.equipment: 1 ball · 2 small goals · Disc cones for outer grid and hotbox square · Pinnies

activities.name: Team Handball
activities.setup: Mark space with 4 cones, goals at each end. Two teams. Players use their hands to pass and catch. They can run with the ball but only for three steps. Score with your feet, but only after a teammate passes you the ball. No dropping to yourself. If the ball hits the ground, goes out, or is intercepted, it is a turnover.
activities.look_for: Using their hands makes it easier for players to keep their heads up and see their teammates' positions. Because scoring requires an assist, combination play is mandatory, not optional. The three-step limit creates natural transition moments. Good final-week activity before the closing game.
activities.question: Because you had to score from a pass, what did you do differently in terms of your positioning than in a normal game?
activities.equipment: 1 ball (any type) · 2 goals · Disc cones · Pinnies

goals.text: Keeps a moving ball close while running
Changes direction without losing control
Looks up sometimes while dribbling, the habit is forming
Receives a short pass and does something intentional with it
Tries to beat defenders rather than just kicking away
Notices teammates and occasionally tries to involve them
Competes with genuine joy and wants to come back next season

who.label: How they learn
who.text: Through experience and repetition, not explanation. Show them a game and they figure it out. Keep instructions short, one idea at a time, then let them play.

who.label: What motivates them
who.text: Scoring goals. Being successful. Having fun with friends. Competing. Keep score. They care about it, and it creates genuine intensity without you manufacturing it.

who.label: Attention and activity
who.text: Their attention span is short but improving. Long lines and waiting kill engagement. Every player should be active for virtually the entire session. If kids are standing still, change the game.

who.label: Positions and the game
who.text: There are no fixed positions at U8. Every player plays everywhere over the course of the season. In the game, rotate the goalkeeper regularly so everyone gets a turn in goal.

great_session.title: Players have the ball constantly
great_session.text: We encourage players to have the ball at their feet as frequently as possible. One player, one ball is the target during practice activities. No sharing, no waiting.

great_session.title: Lots of goals scored
great_session.text: US Soccer is explicit: set up games where players can be successful and score lots of goals. Frequent scoring means high engagement and happy players.

great_session.title: Noise and energy
great_session.text: Laughing, celebrating, competing. If it is quiet, something is wrong. This age group should be loud and joyful.

great_session.title: Coach mostly watching
great_session.text: Your best coaching is a single question after something happens. Resist the urge to over-coach. The game is the teacher.

great_session.title: Players making decisions
great_session.text: Even simple ones: which goal to attack, when to dribble, when to pass. Decision-making in the game starts here.

great_session.title: Sessions end too soon
great_session.text: If players leave wanting more, you did your job. That desire to return is what builds a long-term love of the game.

players.prepared: The best sessions start before the first player arrives. Coaches who show up knowing their activity and their question spend the whole session watching their players and enjoying it. The setup is the same every week: mark a grid with disc cones, lay a ball out for every player, set up cone goals at each end of the closing game space. By the time players arrive, the only thing left to do is put a ball at their feet.

parents.intro: Before the session starts, take 30 seconds to walk over and say something like:
parents.script: Today we are working on keeping the ball close and looking up while dribbling. The most helpful thing you can do is cheer everything: the attempt, the stumble, the scramble. That's the job.
parents.outro: Most parents want to know what is happening and how to help. Give them a role and they will take it. If you see a parent who is genuinely enthusiastic and engaged, that conversation is worth having.

shape.title: The session
shape.note: About 55 to 60 minutes. Arrive 15 minutes early.

opening.label: Opening game
opening.title: Free small-sided game
opening.setup: Same setup every week, so players know this game before they arrive. Mini goals or cone goals at each end. No offside. Ball out of play: restart with a kick-in or dribble-in from the sideline. Set up the space, then step back. Let them play. Restart quickly after every goal. Rotate the goalkeeper throughout the season so every player gets time in the position.
opening.job: Watch. Look for moments of good scanning, a player who tries to beat someone, a clever pass. Make a mental note of two or three things. One of them will tell you which practice activity to run today. Do not stop the game. Do not instruct. Save your voice for the question.
opening.question: Who scored a goal today? How did you do it: did you dribble past someone, or did you find a teammate?
opening.kit: 1 ball per team · Mini goals or cone goals at each end · Disc cones for boundaries · Pinnies in 2 colors

practice.label: Practice
practice.note: Pick one activity based on what you saw in the opening game and run it for 20 to 25 minutes. Rotate through the toolkit across the season.

closing.label: Closing game
closing.title: Back to the game
closing.setup: Same format as the opening. The space can be slightly larger to give players more room. Let it run without stopping and step all the way back. Alternative: one large goal at one end with two cone goals at the halfway line. One team defends the large goal, the other scores through the halfway cones. It gives players a taste of a more directional game.
closing.question: What is one thing you did today that you want to try again next week?
closing.kit: 1 ball per team · Mini goals, cone goals, or 1 large goal plus cone goals · Disc cones for boundaries · Pinnies in 2 colors

cues.say: "Yes, that is scanning. You are already looking for what is next. That is a big deal at any age."

cues.when: Player tries to dribble past and fails
cues.say: "I love that you tried it. What would you do differently next time?"
Celebrate it loudly. Do not over-explain why it worked. Let the result speak for itself.

cues.when: Player stands still without the ball
cues.say: Do not instruct. Ask: "Where could you move to help your team right now?"

cues.when: Player gets frustrated after a mistake
cues.say: "Every player in the world loses the ball. The best ones go and win it straight back."
That is okay. Controlled chaos at U8 is normal. If everyone has a ball and is moving, you are doing it right.

B1.tagline: Keep it close. Head up. Take it with you.
B1.overview: Every player's relationship with the ball comes first. At U8, this block builds comfort and confidence: close touches, moving with the ball, taking on an opponent, and shooting. Heads come up as comfort grows, not before.
B1.problem: Players build the comfort and confidence to move with the ball, take on opponents and shoot, with the ball staying close.
focus: Looking up as ball comfort grows

B2.overview: The first look at team play. Players start to see that a teammate in open space is an option, and that a pass can solve a problem a dribble cannot. At U8 this is low structured: spread out, be available, and pass to a free teammate when it helps.
B2.problem: Players start to use teammates as options: moving into open space to be available, and passing to a free teammate.
focus: Finding open space away from opponents and teammates
Showing the player with the ball an option to pass to

club.contact: Got a question about an activity? Not sure what to run with a particular group? Want to talk through what you are seeing at training? Your Age Group Coordinator and the club Technical Director are there for exactly this. Reach out any time.

who.label: How they have grown
who.text: More sustained attention. They can begin to understand that their actions affect teammates, and they are ready to solve problems together, not just individually.

who.label: What motivates them
who.text: Scoring, competing and belonging. The social side of the game intensifies and they care about their teammates. Celebrate assists as loudly as goals.

who.label: The big shift
who.text: Passing is no longer just an option, it is becoming a tool. Players are beginning to understand that combining with a teammate can beat a defender. That insight is what this year is built around.

who.label: What they are ready for
who.text: 2v1 situations, moving after passing, body shape to receive and basic combination play. Set plays and formations come later. Right now the game itself is the best teacher.

great_session.title: Players move after passing
great_session.text: The give-and-go instinct is forming. Any session where players pass and then stand still is a session where that habit is not developing.

great_session.title: Body shape opens to the field
great_session.text: Players receive with hips at 45-90 degrees toward goal. Name it when you see it. This takes years to become automatic.

great_session.title: 2v1 situations recognized
great_session.text: Players start to sense when a teammate is free. They don't always use it yet. The recognition is the first step.

great_session.title: Players talk to each other
great_session.text: Even one player calling for the ball is a win. Communication starts with the simplest signal.

great_session.title: High energy across both practices
great_session.text: Two practices a week is twice the chance to build habits. Keep both varied and active. The second builds on the first.

great_session.title: Coach with intention
great_session.text: Pick one thing to look for before the session starts. Watch for it. When it happens, ask one good question. That beats a dozen instructions from the sideline.

players.prepared: The best sessions start before the first player arrives. Mark the fields, set up the goals and know your two activities before anyone shows up. Practice A is the familiar anchor. Practice B carries the concept for the week. Know which one you are running.

parents.intro: Before the session, take 30 seconds to walk over and say something like:
parents.script: Today we are working on passing and moving: making a pass and then finding space to get it back. The most helpful thing you can do is cheer when they pass to a teammate, especially if they then keep running.
parents.outro: Most parents want to know what is happening and how to help. Give them a role and they will take it.

B1.tagline: Look up. Open your body. Shoot when you can.
B1.overview: This block builds the individual habits every other block depends on: looking before the ball arrives, opening the body to the field, using the first touch to go forward, and shooting. At U10 the ball also comes under pressure, so the touch has to work with an opponent close by.
B1.problem: Players receive the ball with their head up and body open, use the first touch to go forward, and take on or shoot when it creates danger.
focus: Body open to the field when receiving
First touch that moves the ball toward goal
Dribbling and shooting to create danger

B2.tagline: Pass, move, and be an option.
B2.overview: This is where passing becomes a tool. Players learn that a teammate can solve a problem a dribble cannot. The first habit is the give and go: pass, then move to a new spot to receive again. The second is the 2v1: recognize when a teammate is free and use them to beat a defender.
B2.problem: Players use teammates to beat opponents: passing, then moving to a new position, and creating a 2v1.
focus: Moving after the pass (give and go)
Finding open space and showing the passer

B3.tagline: Close the ball. Cover your teammate.
B3.overview: Defending is a team job. At U10 this block introduces the idea that the nearest player pressures the ball, the next player covers, and the team stays close together. The aim is to stop the opponent from playing forward and win the ball back as high up the field as possible.
B3.problem: Players defend together: the nearest player pressures the ball, a teammate covers, and the team stays close to protect the goal.

weeks.focus: Coach's choice both days
weeks.note: What does your group love most? What do they still need most? Run your two best sessions of the season. Both are correct answers.

goals.text: Keeps the ball under pressure with confidence
Passes and moves without needing to be reminded

who.label: They have been around the game
who.text: Most of these players have been playing for several years. They are still developing their understanding that passing creates space and that defending takes real collective effort. They are ready to be coached on how their individual actions connect to what the team is doing.

who.label: How you deliver feedback matters
who.text: Players at this age are more aware of how they look in front of their peers. When you have something to say to an individual, find something they did right first. Save whole-group feedback for moments of collective success, not individual correction.

who.label: Two practices build habits
who.text: With two sessions a week, what you introduce on day one has time to settle before day two builds on it. Pay attention to what shows up in the second session without you asking for it. That carry-over is the sign the concept is taking hold.

who.label: Ask them why, not just what
who.text: Players at this age can answer deeper questions. "Why does switching the ball make the defender's job harder?" is a question a U12 player can genuinely engage with. Use that.

great_session.title: Immediate reaction to transition
great_session.text: When the ball turns over, do players react instantly? Or do they watch it happen? That first-second reaction is the whole introduction to the game-moments block.

great_session.title: Compact defending shape
great_session.text: Are defenders close enough to support each other? The distance between first and second defender tells you everything about their shape.

great_session.title: Combination play happening naturally
great_session.text: Players who are passing and moving without being asked are showing that the habits from U10 are sticking. If it is not happening yet, go back to a simpler passing activity. The habit builds with repetition.

great_session.title: Players coaching each other
great_session.text: US Soccer notes this explicitly at U12: player-to-player coaching is a development goal, not just a nice thing to see. Step back when it happens.

great_session.title: Practice A concept in Practice B
great_session.text: If a concept introduced in the first session of the week appears in the second session without you asking for it, that is the whole point of two practices a week.

great_session.title: Everyone gets time in goal
great_session.text: Rotate the goalkeeper so every player experiences the position. If someone shows real enthusiasm for it, encourage that too. Positional identity starts forming at this age.

players.prepared: Preparation at U12 matters more than at any previous age. You have four active focuses and a season arc that builds deliberately. Know which focus is the priority for this week before you arrive. With two practices per week, Practice A introduces the concept and Practice B deepens it. If the group needs more time on the same concept before moving forward, run the consolidation instead. Both are correct responses. Try to avoid pairing two new concepts in the same session: Activity A works best as something players already know well enough to run without much explanation, and Activity B is where the new concept lives.

parents.intro: Before the session starts, take 30 seconds to walk over. Something like:
parents.script: Today we are working on what happens when the ball changes hands, in the first second after we win it or lose it. The most helpful thing you can do is cheer the team moments: the player who sprints to press the second they lose the ball, the player who finds a teammate the instant they win it.
parents.outro: At this age players are more aware of what the sideline is saying than they were at U8 or U10. Positive sideline energy is genuinely useful. Critical sideline energy genuinely disrupts.

shape.title: The session
shape.note: Up to 90 minutes. Arrive 15 minutes early. Opening game, Activity A, Activity B, closing game.

opening.label: Opening game
opening.title: 5v5 or 6v6 free small-sided game
opening.setup: Same setup every session. Smaller than the closing game, so more touches and cleaner decisions. Small goals or full goals depending on space. Teams of 5 or 6, no goalkeeper. Quick restarts. Let them play the first 8 minutes without saying anything. On Practice B days, watch specifically for whether the concept from Practice A earlier in the week shows up.
opening.job: Watch the transition moments specifically. What happens in the first couple of seconds after the ball changes hands? That tells you which focus area to prioritize today. Come in with Activity A already chosen and let the opening game confirm your read.
opening.question: When the ball changed hands today, when you won it or lost it, what was your first reaction?
opening.kit: 1 ball per team · Small or full goals · Disc cones · Pinnies in 2 colors

closing.label: Closing game
closing.title: Full game
closing.setup: The biggest game of the session. Proper goals if possible. Include a goalkeeper and rotate it so every player experiences the position across the season. No offside until players are genuinely ready for it. Let the game run without stopping. Watch for the focus you introduced that week showing up without being asked for: a compact defensive shape, or a player who sprints to press the instant possession is lost. On Practice B days, notice whether anything from the first session carried over.
closing.question: Was there a moment today where your whole team did something together, attacking or defending, that one player could not have done alone?
closing.kit: Proper goals if possible · Disc cones · Pinnies in 2 colors

cues.say: "That shape right there, everyone close enough to support each other. That is exactly what we are building toward."
Name it in the moment: "Did everyone see that? No hesitation, immediate reaction. That is what we are building toward."

cues.when: Player switches the point of attack
cues.say: "That pass across the field: what did it do to the defenders? It made them run. That is the whole idea."
Step further back. Let it run. Come back and ask: "What did you tell your teammate there?"

cues.when: Concept from Practice A shows up in Practice B
cues.say: "You did that in the first session this week. Your body remembered. That is exactly what two practices is for."
"The best players in the world make mistakes in every game. The difference is what they do next."

B1.overview: Players know the individual skills from U8 and U10. At U12 they deepen them under more pressure, on a bigger field, with more opponents. Scanning, body shape, first touch, passing range and shooting all get tested at a faster speed.
B1.problem: Players receive, protect and move the ball under real pressure, with their head up and body open.
focus: Passing at the right speed and time

B2.tagline: Pass, move, and switch the picture.
B2.overview: This block goes deeper than U10 as the game gets more complex. Players learn to give the team height, width and depth, to switch the point of attack, to use wall passes in small spaces, and to find the third player.
B2.problem: Players use teammates to move the defense: spreading out, switching the ball and combining to find free players.
focus: Finding free players between the lines

B3.overview: Compact team shape and team defending are reinforced and emphasized from U10. One player pressures the ball, one covers behind, and the rest support to cut off space. Defending moves from individual actions to how the team defends.
B3.problem: Players defend as a team: pressure, cover and support, with a compact shape and a plan for the far side.

B4.overview: This block is introduced at U12. It covers both transition moments: what we do the instant we lose the ball, and the instant we win it. At this age the aim is the habit of reacting at once, not complex decisions.
B4.problem: Players recognize the moment possession changes and react at once, pressing or recovering when it is lost and looking forward when it is won.
focus: First pass forward on winning the ball
